250.t: Kittredge-Waters day job and a rich boy in a poor neighborhood
250.s: His father co-founded the firm he works for; Bergen describes the family house and growing up better off than his friends.
250.q: Yeah, I left Woodward and White. My daddy died in 1938. They needed someone. And I said well I better go where I belong.

624.t: The pie wagon and the blind horse
624.s: Brunies tells of his father selling pies along the riverfront by horse wagon, the saloon-keeper Pick, and the blind horse that brought him home drunk.
624.q: I learned something I want to tell you. Oh, yes. Excuse me. All right. Certainly. My daddy was a patron. Yes. And they used to sell pious under the river. And they used to have a whole fusil.

121.t: Grandfather's sweet potatoes and healthier food
121.s: Digging sweet potatoes and baking them in ashes; thinks the old diet was healthier; hints at a coming hit record.
121.q: Yeah, well, my grandfather, well, we didn't, I didn't have any, we didn't have any room to grow any vegetables, but my grandfather did plant, plant, in his yard there was a gentleman that had a big open field when we were living on Andover Street, right behind, he used to plant sweet potatoes.…

153.t: Italian neighborhoods and his father's music store in Moline
153.s: Recollections of the Italian settlement in Rock Falls where his father taught for tomatoes and wine, the failed restaurant in Peoria, and the full music store in Moline.
153.q: Rock Falls, they had a large Italian settlement there. In fact my dad used to go there just to give lessons. Most of the people were poor. They paid him off by giving him home-grown tomatoes, home-grown wine – grapes. That’s what happened. My recollection of Peoria – we didn’t stay there too long.…

105.t: His father the waiter at the University Club
105.s: Poverty bonded the neighborhood; his father waited tables at the University Club for 49 years, where Hamilton met Earl Warren and Nixon, and his mother stretched two dimes into family meals.
105.q: My father’s occupation, man, he was a professional waiter at the University Club in southern California. Now in order to become -- if you wanted to get into politics you had to become a member of the University Club. When I was a kid, man, I met -- who was the governor that just became -­

672.t: Summers at her grandmother's country home
672.s: Summers were spent picking tomatoes and mushrooms on Whiskey Run Road near her great-grandparents.
672.q: I went to my grandmother’s. Picked tomatoes. Went out in the hollow and picked mushrooms, which I would be scared to death to do today. I wouldn’t have a clue what I was looking for today. It was definitely country. The tomato patch was in the front of the house. My great-grandparents lived across…

145.t: Father's society jobs and a 1926 stag party
145.s: His father played private parties for film people, bankers and real-estate subdivisions, and took the 14-year-old Royal to a Jack Warner stag party where his mother was sent home.
145.ch: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
145.q: would come to school with a bean sandwich, he was pretty poor. Although my dad always provided a little bit better because he was fortunate enough to be able to demand a pretty good salary for his one-nighters and things he did. He didn't work these regular dance halls and things in those days. He…

65.t: Early Havana childhood and the fire in the solar
65.s: He recalls happy Havana, his father selling water glasses, setting fire to the stock, and living in the Jesus Maria solar.
65.q: Well, Havana was so musical, so gay - I mean, so full of life, that I, I don't know, I never had a moment that I, that was a sad moment because that was very happy, very happy era.

409.t: Father's work: furs, then a gambling place on Davis Avenue
409.s: His father bought furs from country trappers, then opened a successful gambling place on Mobile's main street, forbidding Cootie to go near it.
409.q: I didn't ever get to look at it. I knew where it was situated, but he didn't allow me in the pool room.

18.t: Farm chores, watermelon patch and his father's 365 acres
18.s: He rode cows, grew watermelons on an acre his father gave him, and says his father had 365 acres.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: (NOT CLEAR) ...I paid the guys off in watermelons. Every Saturday we would be off... So I had my watermelon patch and every time we'd get the watermelons we'd take them down - and the dam is still there, it's still there, and the walk over it. You know, I'm going to Aunt Jessie's or Aunt Margaret's…

235.t: Aunt Rebecca, Uncle Charles and the fight in the courtyard
235.s: He recalls his aunt and uncle and a childhood fight in a courtyard like Catfish Row.
235.q: Oh, my uncle and my aunt, I didn't know too much, that was vague, but they were very nice, you know, but...hmmmm, my aunt's name was Rebecca and my uncle's name was Charles. They were very nice, I remember them. I'll never forget, I got in a fight one day and this great big guy, he said something,…

31.t: Fish Whaley, learning to swim, and his father's good earnings
31.s: Whaley says he was nicknamed Fish for swimming underwater, and describes his Everett playground, his father's hotel tips and the children's good clothes.
31.q: And Thomas Whaley, right. Tom Whaley. They used to call me Fish Whaley, because they said I could swim underwater longer than anybody else.

79.t: His parents' permission; walking home at night
79.s: His mother made him wait for his father, who finally gave permission. Thomas, at 12 or 13, walked home alone through the quiet country at night.
79.ch: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work
79.q: particular day I met my dad which I'd never done before. So he said, "Well, hi Joe." I say, "Hi, Pop." He said, "Well, what did you meet me for?" So I explained to him and he didn't say anything. He said, "Well, I got to talk to your mother." See my father and I could always get together I thought…
